claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments in Rb-inactive cell lines showing similar size homeostasis mechanisms.

claims.claim: Perturbing Cdk4 activity influences cell size.
claims.source: Additionally, although Rb signaling is not required for these regulatory behaviors, perturbing Cdk4 activity still influences cell size, suggesting that the Cdk4 pathway may play a role in designating the cell's target size.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by palbociclib treatment and cyclin D overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: The Cdk4 pathway may play a role in designating the cell's target size.
claims.source: Additionally, although Rb signaling is not required for these regulatory behaviors, perturbing Cdk4 activity still influences cell size, suggesting that the Cdk4 pathway may play a role in designating the cell's target size.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the abstract based on the differential effects of Cdk4 versus other Cdk inhibitors.

claims.claim: Uniformity of cell size is a consistent feature of healthy tissues.
claims.source: Uniformity of cell size is a consistent feature of healthy tissues.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the introduction.

claims.claim: Different cell types can differ greatly in size, but cells within a given tissue tend to be strikingly similar.
claims.source: While different cell types can differ greatly in size, cells within a given tissue tend to be strikingly similar (Ginzberg et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an established observation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In some tissues, loss of cell size uniformity is a diagnostic marker of malignancy.
claims.source: In fact, in some tissues, loss of cell size uniformity is a diagnostic marker of malignancy (Greenough, 1925).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an established clinical observation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Evidence of cell size checkpoints in the cell cycle of both budding yeast and fission yeast was first reported in 1977.
claims.source: Evidence of cell size checkpoints in the cell cycle of both budding yeast and fission yeast was first reported in 1977 (Johnston et al., 1977; Fantes and Nurse, 1977).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations.

claims.claim: In both budding and fission yeast, the length of the cell cycle is selectively extended in small cells.
claims.source: In both species, it was found that the length of the cell cycle is selectively extended in small cells, giving them more time to grow before their next division.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an established finding from yeast studies.

claims.claim: Two classes of models have been proposed to explain the biophysical basis of size sensing in yeast: geometric models and titration-based models.
claims.source: Two classes of models have been proposed to explain the biophysical basis of size sensing in yeast (Wood and Nurse, 2015). Geometric models propose that cells measure dimensions such as cell length or surface area by relying on highly specific intracellular localizations of cell-cycle regulators such as pom1 or cdr2 (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Bhatia et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2014). Alternatively, titration-based models suggest that the concentration of a cell cycle activator overcomes the concentration of a cell cycle inhibitor in a growth-dependent manner (Turner et al., 2012; Schmoller et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Several studies have suggested that the cell cycle of animal cells includes cell size checkpoints.
claims.source: Several studies have suggested that the cell cycle of animal cells, like that of yeast, also includes cell size checkpoints (Killander and Zetterberg, 1965a; Dolznig et al., 2004; Gao and Raff, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citations.

claims.claim: In 1965, Zetterberg and Killander reported that proliferating fibroblasts that have recently entered S-phase are more uniform in size than sister cells that have just exited mitosis.
claims.source: In 1965, Zetterberg and Killander reported that proliferating fibroblasts that have recently entered S-phase are more uniform in size than sister cells that have just exited mitosis (Killander and Zetterberg, 1965a).
claims.evidence: This is a historical finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Zetterberg and Killander concluded that cells that are smaller than a critical size are maintained in G1 for longer periods of growth.
claims.source: Based on these and other observations, they concluded that cells that are smaller than a critical size are maintained in G1 for longer periods of growth (Killander and Zetterberg, 1965b).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from prior work supported by citation.

claims.claim: The restriction point is the time early in G1 when cells commit to undergoing another cell division cycle if growth factors are present.
claims.source: A defining event in the eukaryotic cell cycle is the 'restriction point', the time early in G1 when cells commit to undergoing another cell division cycle if growth factors are present (or transition to a quiescent G0 state in the absence of growth factors) (Pardee, 1974).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle biology supported by citation.

claims.claim: In budding yeast, some studies suggest that the restriction point (START) and the cell size checkpoint are one and the same.
claims.source: In budding yeast, some studies suggest that the restriction point (START) and the cell size checkpoint are one and the same (Cross, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work supported by citation.

claims.claim: Research addressing whether animal cells autonomously sense and regulate their own size remains inconclusive.
claims.source: Despite the studies described above, research addressing the question of whether animal cells, like yeast, autonomously sense and regulate their own size remains inconclusive (Lloyd, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Two alternate models have been proposed to explain cell size homeostasis: the adder model and the sizer model.
claims.source: Since the 1960s, two alternate models have been proposed to explain cell size homeostasis, the adder model and the sizer model (Conlon and Raff, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature with supporting citation.

claims.claim: According to the adder model, size homeostasis is not the result of size-sensing mechanisms but the outcome of a balance between constant mass accumulation and mass reduction at division.
claims.source: According to the adder model, size homeostasis is not the result of size-sensing mechanisms. Instead, size homeostasis is the outcome of a balance between a constant amount of mass that cells accumulate each cell cycle and the reduction in cell mass that accompanies cell division.
claims.evidence: This is a description of an existing theoretical model.

claims.claim: The adder model assumes that small and large cells accumulate the same amount of mass over the course of the cell cycle.
claims.source: At the core of the adder model is the assumption that small and large cells accumulate the same amount of mass over the course of the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a key assumption of the adder model.

claims.claim: The sizer model assumes that size homeostasis is the product of size-sensing mechanisms that selectively restrict the growth of large cells or promote the growth of small cells.
claims.source: In contrast to the adder model, the sizer model assumes that size homeostasis is the product of size-sensing mechanisms that selectively restrict the growth of large cells or promote the growth of small cells.
claims.evidence: This is a description of an existing theoretical model.

claims.claim: Most cells in an animal body are terminally differentiated and do not undergo cell cycles, yet still display size uniformity.
claims.source: In animals, most cells are terminally differentiated. These cells do not divide and yet, often undergo precise adjustments of cell size (Nie et al., 2013). Also, it is often in such terminally differentiated tissues that size uniformity is most striking.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cell size is defined in this study as a cell's total macromolecular protein mass.
claims.source: In this study, we define cell size by a cell's total macromolecular protein mass, as this metric most closely reflects the sum of anabolic processes typically associated with cell growth (Mitchison, 2003) and with activity in growth-promoting pathways such as mTORC1 (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an explicit methodological definition stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Cell volume is a more labile phenotype than protein mass, sensitive to ion channel regulation and fluctuations in extracellular osmolarity.
claims.source: In contrast, cell volume is a more labile phenotype, sensitive to ion channel regulation and fluctuations in extracellular osmolarity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a justification for using protein mass rather than volume.

claims.claim: SE-A647 staining is sensitive enough to detect the change in cell mass that occurs in less than three hours of growth.
claims.source: SE-A647 staining is sensitive enough to detect the change in cell mass that occurs in less than three hours of growth (less than 15% of the cell cycle) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: S-phase cells are significantly larger than G1 cells of the same age in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the existence of a cell size checkpoint (Figure 1B), Figure 1D shows that S-phase cells are significantly larger than G1 cells of the same age, even though both have been growing for the same amount of time since birth. This suggests that cells exit G1 in a size-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The mean size of G1 cells plateaus as cells begin to enter S-phase.
claims.source: Furthermore, the mean size of G1 cells plateaus as cells begins to enter S-phase, consistent with a mechanism where cells enter S-phase upon reaching a particular size threshold.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The size difference between identically aged G1 and S-phase cells is statistically significant (p<3.92e-04).
claims.source: The size difference between identically aged G1 and S-phase cells is statistically significant (student's t-test p<3.92e-04) and was observed in three additional independent replicate experiments (p<0.009, p<5.80e-08, p<9.07e-15).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: In yeast, the nucleus grows continuously throughout all stages of cell cycle and is correlated with cell size.
claims.source: In yeast, the nucleus is known to grow continuously throughout all stages of cell cycle and is correlated with cell size (Jorgensen et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from yeast studies with supporting citation.

claims.claim: There is a significant correlation (Pearson's r = 0.68) between nucleus size and cell size in HeLa cells.
claims.source: As expected, this correlation is significant (Pearson's r = 0.68).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Both cell size and nucleus size continually increase throughout the cell cycle.
claims.source: Figure 2B and C show that both cell size and nucleus size continually increase throughout the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: Growth in nucleus size is independent of DNA synthesis.
claims.source: Last, we confirmed that growth in nucleus size is independent of DNA synthesis, by treating cells with aphidicolin to prevent DNA replication. Aphidicolin-arrested cells continued to grow in both cell size and nucleus size (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), maintaining a correlation between the two.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: There is a significant negative correlation (Pearson's r = −0.41, p=6.7 x 10−8) between nucleus size at birth and G1 duration in HeLa cells.
claims.source: When we monitored nuclear growth in single cells expressing nuclear-localized cell cycle markers, we observed a significant and reproducible negative correlation between the size of the nucleus at birth and G1 duration (Figure 2D). Hela cells that had smaller nuclei at birth spent longer amounts of time in G1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Culturing Rpe1 cells in 70 nM rapamycin for several days caused a 60% decrease in the average growth rate.
claims.source: Culturing Rpe1 cells in 70 nM rapamycin for several days caused a 60% decrease in the average growth rate.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment caused an 80% increase in the average G1 duration of Rpe1 cells.
claims.source: As predicted, we observed an 80% increase in the average G1 duration of these cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The profound effect of rapamycin on growth rate caused only a 20% reduction in cell size due to the lengthened cell cycle.
claims.source: Because of the lengthened cell cycle, the profound effect of rapamycin on growth rate caused only a 20% reduction in cell size (Figure 3A–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The influence of rapamycin on G1 length may be an indirect consequence of its influence on growth rate.
claims.source: Our current results suggest that the influence of rapamycin on G1 length may be an indirect consequence of its influence on growth rate. According to this interpretation, the inhibition of cell growth by rapamycin results in a gradual reduction of cell size which, in turn, triggers compensatory increases in G1 length.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Cell size variance can only decrease if small cells grow faster than large cells.
claims.source: In fact, in a synchronized population of growing cells, variance in size can only decrease if small cells grow faster than large cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical statement derived from the variance equation presented in the text.

claims.claim: Periods of decreasing cell size variance occur during the cell cycle of unperturbed HeLa and Rpe1 cells.
claims.source: Figure 4 shows that periods of decreasing cell size variance do, in fact, occur during the cell cycle of unperturbed HeLa and Rpe1 cells (Figure 4C–F). During these periods, cells grow (mean size increases), and yet become more similar in size. This indicates that cellular growth rates are regulated to correct aberrant cell sizes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claims.claim: The observation of at least two periods during which Gcv is negative is highly reproducible.
claims.source: While the exact timing of the drops in Gcv varied between experiments (and a third, weaker drop is occasionally observed in HeLa cells), the observation of at least two periods during which Gcv is negative is highly reproducible.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a reproducible finding from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: Growth rates of individual cells become slower in large cells and faster in small cells, causing cells that were initially quite different in size to gradually become more uniform.
claims.source: Because growth rates became slower in large cells and faster in small cells, individual cells that were initially quite different in size gradually become more uniform in size, explaining the decreases in cell size variance shown in Figure 4E–H.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Perturbations that lengthen the cell cycle would be counteracted by a compensatory decrease in growth rate.
claims.source: A prediction of this dual-mechanism model is that perturbations that lengthen the cell cycle would be counteracted by a compensatory decrease in growth rate, allowing cells to accumulate the same amount of mass despite the longer periods of growth.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the dual-mechanism model.

claims.claim: Perturbations that reduce growth rate would be counteracted by a compensatory lengthening of G1.
claims.source: Conversely, perturbations that reduce growth rate would be counteracted by a compensatory lengthening of G1.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the dual-mechanism model.

claims.claim: SNS-032 treatment caused an increase in average cell size in Rpe1 cells.
claims.source: Figure 6A (top panel) shows the influence of the growth rate inhibitor (rapamycin) and the cell cycle inhibitor (SNS-032) on Rpe1 cell size. While SNS-032 treatment caused an increase in average cell size, rapamycin treatment caused a decrease in average cell size.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment caused a decrease in average cell size in Rpe1 cells.
claims.source: Figure 6A (top panel) shows the influence of the growth rate inhibitor (rapamycin) and the cell cycle inhibitor (SNS-032) on Rpe1 cell size. While SNS-032 treatment caused an increase in average cell size, rapamycin treatment caused a decrease in average cell size.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: For both SNS-032 and rapamycin, the change in average cell size proceeded only during the initial phase of drug treatment, followed by stabilization of a new cell size.
claims.source: For both drugs, the change in average cell size proceeded only during the initial phase of drug treatment, followed by stabilization of a new cell size that no longer changed with time.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: SNS-032 caused an immediate decrease in proliferation rate.
claims.source: As expected, the Cdk2 inhibitor SNS-032 caused an immediate decrease in proliferation rate.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Rapamycin's influence on proliferation rate occurred only during the late stage of drug treatment.
claims.source: Notably, while rapamycin also slowed proliferation rate, this influence only occurred during the late stage of drug treatment.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment induced an immediate effect on cell size.
claims.source: In contrast, rapamycin treatment induced an immediate effect on cell size.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The influence of cdk2 inhibitor SNS-032 on growth rate is indirect and is mediated by a property that accumulates over time, presumably cell size.
claims.source: Specifically, while SNS-032 caused an immediate lengthening of cell cycle, its influence on growth rate was observed only after prolonged drug treatment (Figure 6B,E and F). This suggests that the influence of cdk2 inhibitor SNS-032 on growth rate is indirect and is mediated by a property that accumulates over time, presumable cell size.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the temporal order of effects shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Rapamycin caused an immediate reduction in growth rate, while its influence on cell cycle length occurred much later.
claims.source: Conversely, rapamycin caused an immediate reduction in growth rate, while its influence on cell cycle length occurred much later (Figure 6B–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claims.claim: Most chemical perturbations of growth rate and cell cycle length had surprisingly small influences on Rpe1 cell size.
claims.source: Figure 7A and B show that most chemical perturbations of growth rate and cell cycle length had surprisingly small influences on Rpe1 cell size. Whiles drugs produced up to 4-fold changes in both growth rate and cell cycle length, the largest changes in cell size were close to 1-fold (i.e. 50% change in cell size), with most treatments changing size by less than 30%.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claims.claim: Treatment with all but one (palbociclib) of the tested compounds resulted in coordinated changes of both cell cycle length and growth rate, such that cell size remained relatively unchanged.
claims.source: Consistent with the dual-mechanism model, treatment with all but one (palbociclib, Figure 8A) of the tested compounds resulted in coordinated changes of both cell cycle length and growth rate, such that cell size remained relatively unchanged.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Growth rate inhibitors caused a small decrease in cell size.
claims.source: Also, consistent with the results in Figure 6, growth rate inhibitors caused a small decrease in cell size (Figure 7A, rightmost panel) while cell cycle inhibitors caused a small increase in cell size (Figure 7B, rightmost panel).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Cell cycle inhibitors caused a small increase in cell size.
claims.source: Also, consistent with the results in Figure 6, growth rate inhibitors caused a small decrease in cell size (Figure 7A, rightmost panel) while cell cycle inhibitors caused a small increase in cell size (Figure 7B, rightmost panel).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Inhibitors of cell cycle regulators cause immediate lengthening of the cell cycle followed by compensatory decreases in growth rate.
claims.source: Lastly, separate analysis of early and late stages of the drug treatments confirmed that inhibitors of cell cycle regulators cause immediate lengthening of the cell cycle followed by compensatory decreases in growth rate, while cycloheximide, torin-2, and rapamycin induce immediate decreases in growth rate followed by compensatory increases in cell cycle length (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide, torin-2, and rapamycin induce immediate decreases in growth rate followed by compensatory increases in cell cycle length.
claims.source: Lastly, separate analysis of early and late stages of the drug treatments confirmed that inhibitors of cell cycle regulators cause immediate lengthening of the cell cycle followed by compensatory decreases in growth rate, while cycloheximide, torin-2, and rapamycin induce immediate decreases in growth rate followed by compensatory increases in cell cycle length (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Only the cdk4/6 inhibitor palbociclib increased cell cycle length without triggering a compensatory decrease in growth rate, causing an unusual increase in cell size.
claims.source: Of the tested cdk inhibitors, only the cdk4/6 inhibitor palbociclib increased cell cycle length without triggering a compensatory decrease in growth rate, causing an unusual increase in cell size (Figure 8A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of cdk4 and cdk6 by siRNA yielded a similar increase in cell size as palbociclib treatment.
claims.source: Knockdown of cdk4 and cdk6 by siRNA yielded a similar increase in cell size (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Culturing cells in radicicol not only decoupled growth rate and cell cycle length but also increased cell size variability by 26% (±3.2%) relative to untreated cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, culturing cells in radicicol not only decoupled growth rate and cell cycle length (Figure 8A,B), but also increased cell size variability by 26% (±3.2%) relative to untreated cells (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claims.claim: Cdk4/6 inhibition with palbociclib had no significant influence on cell size heterogeneity.
claims.source: In contrast, cdk4/6 inhibition with palbociclib had no significant influence on cell size heterogeneity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as a comparison to radicicol treatment.

claims.claim: Cell size uniformity is a regulated phenotype that can be perturbed by disrupting the coordination of growth and cell cycle progression.
claims.source: This finding further illustrates that cell size uniformity is a regulated phenotype that can be perturbed by disrupting the coordination of growth and cell cycle progression.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the radicicol results.

claims.claim: The reciprocal influence of various drug treatments on growth rate and cell cycle length in Rpe1 cells match the trend predicted by the equation v = C_TS / τ.
claims.source: Figure 9A shows that the reciprocal influence of the various drug treatments on growth rate and cell cycle length in Rpe1 cells match the trend predicted by Equation 5.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The intact size compensation in Rb-inactive cell lines suggests that, while the cyclin D-Rb axis plays a role in specifying the target cell size, this pathway is not responsible for the coordination of growth rate with cell cycle length to maintain cell size uniformity.
claims.source: The intact size compensation in Rb-inactive cell lines suggests that, while the cyclin D-Rb axis plays a role in specifying the target cell size, this pathway is not responsible for the coordination of growth rate with cell cycle length to maintain cell size uniformity.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on experiments in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Overexpression of cyclin E shortened the cell cycle, but the size distribution of cells overexpressing cyclin E was indistinguishable from control cells due to a compensatory increase in growth rate.
claims.source: While overexpression of cyclin E shortened the cell cycle, the size distribution of cells overexpressing cyclin E was indistinguishable from control cells (Figure 10A,D), due to a compensatory increase in growth rate (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 10A, D and Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of p27 lengthened the duration of cell cycle, but cells overexpressing p27 were only minimally different in size.
claims.source: Similarly, while overexpression of p27 lengthened the duration of cell cycle, cells overexpressing p27 were only minimally different in size (Figure 10C,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 10C and F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of cyclin D caused a shortening of cell cycle that was accompanied by dramatic reduction in cell size.
claims.source: In contrast, overexpression of cyclin D caused a shortening of cell cycle that was accompanied by dramatic reduction in cell size (Figure 10B,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 10B and E.

claims.claim: The ability of cells to compensate for genetic perturbations of cyclin E but not for perturbations of cyclin D is consistent with pharmacological perturbations and suggests a distinct role for cyclin D/Cdk4 in target size regulation.
claims.source: The ability of cells to compensate for genetic perturbations of cyclin E but not for perturbations of cyclin D is consistent with our pharmacological perturbations and suggests a distinct role for cyclin D/Cdk4 in target size regulation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the cyclin overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: The results refute the premise that cell size is simply the quotient of independently regulated rates of cell growth and division.
claims.source: The results presented here refute the premise that cell size is simply the quotient of independently regulated rates of cell growth and division (Lloyd, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: There is feedback between cell growth and cell cycle progression that robustly maintains cell size even in the face of strong perturbations.
claims.source: Instead, we show evidence of feedback between these two processes that robustly maintains cell size even in the face of strong perturbations of either growth or cell cycle progression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: The presence of feedback that maintains a constant cell size and minimizes variation in cell size suggests the presence of a cell size sensor.
claims.source: The presence of feedback that maintains a constant cell size, and minimizes variation in cell size, suggests the presence of a cell size sensor.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: The correlation of nucleus area and G1 length is statistically significant (p<6.7×10−8) and reproducible (N > 4).
claims.source: While the correlation of nucleus area and G1 length is statistically significant (p<6.7×10−8, Figure 2D) and reproducible (N > 4), it is not a strong correlation (Pearson's r = −0.41).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: Correction of fluctuations in cell size by mechanisms other than cell cycle checkpoints would tend to loosen the demand on the G1-length extension mechanism and weaken the correlation between cell size and G1 length.
claims.source: As is elaborated in the discussion, correction of fluctuations in cell size by mechanisms other than cell cycle checkpoints would tend to loosen the demand on the G1-length extension mechanism and weaken the correlation between cell size and G1 length.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text to explain the weak correlation.

claims.claim: The size threshold model is fundamentally limited in its ability to correct the size of very large cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, the size threshold model is fundamentally limited in its ability to correct the size of very large cells. If some cells grow fast enough to double even in a very short cell cycle, regulation of cell cycle length alone cannot constrain size variability in the population.
claims.evidence: This is a logical argument stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Cells that are smaller than their target size grow faster and for longer periods of time.
claims.source: Cells that are smaller than their target size grow faster and for longer periods of time.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: Cell size is strongly influenced by the Rb/cyclin D axis.
claims.source: These results are also consistent with the dramatic influence of Cln3 (a cyclin D homologue) on cell size in budding yeast (Tyers et al., 1992). Altogether, these results suggest that cell size is strongly influenced by the Rb/cyclin D axis.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion based on the palbociclib and cyclin D overexpression results, with supporting citation.

claims.claim: Rb is not required for maintenance of size homeostasis, nor for the coordination of growth rate with cell cycle length.
claims.source: On one hand, Figure 9 shows that Rb is not required for maintenance of size homeostasis, nor for the coordination of growth rate with cell size length.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on experiments in Rb-inactive cell lines shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The dramatic influence of cyclin D/Cdk4 on cell size implies an important role for the Rb-cyclin D axis in size regulation.
claims.source: On the other hand, the dramatic influence of cyclin D/Cdk4 on cell size (Figure 8, Figure 10) implies an important role for the Rb-cyclin D axis in size regulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the palbociclib and cyclin D overexpression results.

claims.claim: The function of the Rb-cyclin D axis may be in dictating the specific cell size value (i.e. 'target size') to be maintained rather than in ensuring cell size homeostasis at that target size.
claims.source: An intriguing possibility is that the function of the Rb-cyclin D axis is in dictating the specific cell size value (i.e. 'target size') to be maintained rather than in ensuring cell size homeostasis at that target size.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Palbociclib causes a relatively uniform increase in cell size, suggesting a reprogramming of target size.
claims.source: Consistent with the possibility that Cdk4 is involved in target size specification, palbociclib, a cdk4/6 inhibitor, causes a relatively uniform increase in cell size, suggesting a reprograming of target size.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion based on the palbociclib results.

claims.claim: The size increase caused by radicicol is accompanied by an increase in the variability of cell size, suggesting a disruption of cell size homeostasis.
claims.source: In contrast, the size increase caused by radicicol, an hsp90 inhibitor, is accompanied by an increase in the variability of cell size, suggesting a disruption of cell size homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion based on the radicicol results.

claims.claim: SE-A647 staining is an accurate measure of cell mass.
claims.source: At the end of the imaging session, cells were immediately fixed and stained with AlexaFluor 647-Succinimidyl Ester (SE-A647), a quantitative protein stain that we previously established as a an accurate measure of cell mass (Kafri et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an established method with supporting citation.

claims.claim: The average size of the oldest cells is approximately double that of the youngest cells.
claims.source: As expected, the average size of the oldest cells is approximately double that of the youngest.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The transient slowing of cell growth about 10 hr after birth is consistent with a behavior previously identified.
claims.source: The transient slowing of cell growth about 10 hr after birth (the average age of S-phase entry) is consistent with a behavior we and others have previously identified (Kafri et al., 2013; Gut et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text with supporting citations and can be observed in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The size distribution of mitotics is identical to that of the oldest cells tracked.
claims.source: The size distribution of mitotics is identical to that of the oldest cells tracked, confirming that the data in Figure 1C represents growth over the course of the entire cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The mean age of mitotic cells is 21 hr, with a standard deviation of 1.6 hr.
claims.source: The mean age of mitotic cells is 21 hr, with a standard deviation of 1.6 hr.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The correlation between log(growth rate) and log(cell cycle length) in Rpe1 cells treated with growth or cell cycle inhibitors (excluding palbociclib and radicicol) and cyclin E1 overexpression is r = −0.76, p=2.1×10−7.
claims.source: Calculation of the Pearson correlation coefficient between log(growth rate) and log(cell cycle length), using data from conditions marked by gray circles (inhibition of growth or cell cycle progression) and green diamond (cyclin E1 overexpression), yields r = −0.76, p=2.1×10−7, by two-tailed Student's t-test, indicating a significant inverse correlation between growth rate and cell cycle length in these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result stated in the text and shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: When rapamycin is used to slow growth, the slope of nucleus size versus G1 length becomes about 50% steeper.
claims.source: In support of this idea, we repeatedly observe that when growth is inhibited with rapamycin the slope of nucleus size versus G1 length becomes about 50% steeper (See Liu et. al., Figure 3G versus 3I [Liu et al., 2018]).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to a related study.

results.result: S-phase cells are significantly larger than G1 cells of the same age in HeLa cells, with the mean size of G1 cells plateauing as cells enter S-phase, consistent with a size-dependent G1/S transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide converging evidence for a cell size checkpoint at G1/S transition. The statistical significance (p<3.92e-04) is robust and reproduced across multiple replicates. The plateau in G1 cell size at S-phase entry time supports the size threshold model. The data in Figure 1D clearly demonstrates the predicted pattern.

results.result: There is a significant but weak negative correlation (Pearson's r = −0.41, p=6.7×10⁻⁸) between nucleus size at birth and G1 duration in HeLa cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C35 and C80 establish a statistically significant correlation that is reproducible (N>4). While the correlation is weak (r=-0.41), the authors acknowledge this and provide a plausible explanation (C81) that other size correction mechanisms reduce the demand on G1-length extension. The statistical significance is strong despite the weak correlation coefficient.

results.result: Rapamycin treatment causes a 60% decrease in growth rate and 80% increase in G1 duration, resulting in only a 20% reduction in cell size, suggesting that rapamycin's effect on G1 length is an indirect consequence of its effect on growth rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 provide quantitative data showing compensatory changes in G1 length that buffer cell size from growth rate perturbations. The interpretation in C39 is reasonable given the temporal dynamics shown in Figure 6 and is consistent with the size-sensing model. The small change in cell size despite large changes in growth rate and cell cycle length supports the dual-mechanism model.

results.result: Periods of decreasing cell size variance occur twice during the cell cycle of unperturbed HeLa and Rpe1 cells, during which growth rates become slower in large cells and faster in small cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C44, and C45 are supported by the Gcv analysis (Figure 4) and direct observation of nuclear growth trajectories (Figure 4I). The reproducibility across multiple experiments and two cell lines strengthens the finding. The mathematical derivation underlying the Gcv analysis is sound, and the direct visualization confirms the inference.

results.result: SNS-032 (Cdk2 inhibitor) causes immediate cell cycle lengthening followed by delayed growth rate reduction, while rapamycin causes immediate growth rate reduction followed by delayed cell cycle lengthening, with both effects mediated by changes in cell size.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 describe temporal dynamics that support the dual-mechanism model. The separation of early and late effects (Figure 6) provides strong evidence that the compensatory responses are mediated by cell size changes. The contrasting temporal order of effects between SNS-032 and rapamycin is particularly compelling evidence for size-dependent feedback.

results.result: Most chemical perturbations of growth rate and cell cycle length produce coordinated reciprocal changes such that cell size remains relatively unchanged, with growth rate inhibitors causing small decreases and cell cycle inhibitors causing small increases in cell size.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 demonstrate the robustness of size homeostasis across multiple perturbations (Figure 7). The systematic testing of multiple drugs at multiple concentrations, with temporal analysis of early and late effects, provides strong support. The consistency of the pattern across different perturbations strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Palbociclib (Cdk4/6 inhibitor) uniquely increases cell size without compensatory growth rate reduction, while radicicol disrupts size homeostasis by increasing both cell size and size variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 identify exceptions to the general pattern that reveal mechanistic insights. The genetic validation with siRNA (C66) strengthens the palbociclib finding. The quantified increase in size variability with radicicol (26% ± 3.2%) versus no change with palbociclib provides clear evidence for distinct mechanisms. These exceptions are well-documented in Figures 8 and 9.

results.result: The reciprocal relationship between growth rate and cell cycle length follows the predicted equation v = C_TS/τ across multiple cell lines, with a significant inverse correlation (r = −0.76, p=2.1×10⁻⁷) in Rpe1 cells, and this coordination is maintained in Rb-inactive cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C72, and C96 demonstrate quantitative agreement with the theoretical model across five cell lines (Figure 9). The strong correlation coefficient and highly significant p-value support the mathematical relationship. The finding that Rb-inactive cell lines maintain size compensation (C72) is important for distinguishing target size specification from size homeostasis mechanisms.

results.result: Overexpression of cyclin E or p27 produces compensatory changes in growth rate that maintain cell size, while cyclin D overexpression causes dramatic size reduction without compensation, suggesting a distinct role for cyclin D/Cdk4 in target size regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 provide genetic validation of the pharmacological findings. The contrast between cyclin E (compensated) and cyclin D (not compensated) is clear in Figure 10. The interpretation (C76) is consistent with the palbociclib results and supported by the data, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Nucleus size correlates significantly with cell size (r = 0.68) and both increase continuously throughout the cell cycle, with nuclear growth independent of DNA synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 validate nucleus size as a proxy for cell size. The correlation is significant and the aphidicolin experiment (C34, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) demonstrates that nuclear growth is independent of DNA replication. This validation is essential for the live-cell tracking experiments.

results.result: SE-A647 staining is sensitive enough to detect cell mass changes occurring in less than three hours of growth and is an accurate measure of cell mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C90 establish the validity of the primary measurement method. The sensitivity is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and the method was previously validated (Kafri et al., 2013). This is essential methodological validation but not a primary finding of this study.

results.result: Cell size approximately doubles over the cell cycle, with a transient slowing of growth around S-phase entry at ~10 hours, and mean cell cycle length of 21 hours with standard deviation of 1.6 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93, C95 provide basic characterization of cell growth and cell cycle timing. These are well-supported by the data in Figures 1 and 4, and the transient growth slowing is consistent with prior work (C92). These are descriptive findings that provide context for the main results.

results.result: Cell size variance can only decrease if small cells grow faster than large cells, as derived from the mathematical relationship between variance and covariance of size and growth rate.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 presents a mathematical derivation that is logically sound and correctly derived from Equations 1-2 in the manuscript. This mathematical framework is essential for the Gcv analysis method but is a theoretical result rather than an experimental finding.

results.result: The dual-mechanism model predicts that perturbations lengthening the cell cycle would be counteracted by decreased growth rate, and perturbations reducing growth rate would be counteracted by lengthened G1.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 state predictions that are logical consequences of the dual-mechanism model. These predictions are subsequently tested and confirmed by the experimental data in Figures 6-7, but the claims themselves are theoretical predictions rather than experimental results.

results.result: The results refute the premise that cell size is simply the quotient of independently regulated growth and division rates, instead demonstrating feedback between these processes and suggesting the presence of a cell size sensor.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C83 are high-level conclusions drawn from the collective experimental evidence. While these interpretations are well-supported by the data, they are synthetic conclusions rather than individual experimental results. The inference of a size sensor (C79) is reasonable but the sensor itself is not identified.

results.result: Perturbing Cdk4 activity influences cell size, with the Cdk4/cyclin D/Rb axis potentially playing a role in designating target size rather than maintaining size homeostasis, as evidenced by palbociclib causing uniform size increases and radicicol causing increased size variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C84, C86-C89 propose a specific role for Cdk4 in target size specification. The experimental evidence (palbociclib, cyclin D overexpression, Rb-inactive cell lines) supports this interpretation, though the claims acknowledge this is speculative (C7, C87). The distinction between target size specification and size homeostasis is conceptually important and supported by the differential effects of Cdk4 versus other Cdk inhibitors.

results.result: Rb signaling is not required for cell size regulatory behaviors or for coordination of growth rate with cell cycle length, as demonstrated by intact size compensation in Rb-inactive cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C85 are supported by experiments in multiple Rb-inactive cell lines (SAOS2, HeLa, 16HBE) showing similar coordination patterns as Rb-active lines (Figure 9). This is an important negative result that helps distinguish the roles of different cell cycle regulators in size control.

results.result: Correction of cell size fluctuations by mechanisms other than cell cycle checkpoints would weaken the correlation between cell size and G1 length, and the size threshold model is fundamentally limited in correcting very large cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 provide logical arguments explaining limitations of single-mechanism models. C81 explains the weak correlation observed in C35/C80, and C82 identifies a theoretical limitation of checkpoint-only models. These are valid logical inferences that support the dual-mechanism model, though they are not direct experimental results.

results.result: When rapamycin is used to slow growth, the slope of nucleus size versus G1 length becomes about 50% steeper.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 cites data from a companion study (Liu et al., 2018) showing that inhibiting growth rate regulation increases reliance on G1-length extension. This supports the interpretation in C81 but is not a primary result of this manuscript.

results.result: Cells employ two strategies to maintain appropriate size: adjusting both cell cycle length and growth rate, with growth rates selectively increased in small cells and reduced in large cells twice during the cell cycle, and cell-size-dependent adjustments of G1 length further reducing variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 summarize the main findings stated in the abstract. These are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript (Figures 1-10). C1 is a motivating observation, while C2-C4 are primary conclusions supported by multiple lines of evidence.
